m2c/src/m2c/policy/__init__.py -- Patch C06: the policy engine v0.

    modes.py       the modes ``plan`` / ``ask`` / ``accept-edits``, the tool
                   catalog (a copy of protocol/v1/tools) and the default decision
                   per mode, tool class and risk
    rules.py       ``allow`` / ``ask`` / ``deny`` rules as ``tool(pattern)``, the
                   managed > user > project layers, the loader, and the lexical
                   path checks (protected paths, the secrets denylist)
    shellparse.py  a real tokenizer for the shell subset that matters; whatever
                   it cannot classify with certainty is "unknown syntax" (ask)
    decide.py      ``decide(request, context) -> Decision``: pure, total, and
                   fail closed

Typical use::

    from m2c.policy import Context, Request, load_layers
    from m2c.policy.decide import decide

    layers = load_layers(managed=None, user=config_dir / "settings.toml",
                         project=root / ".m2c" / "settings.toml",
                         project_trusted=trusted)
    d = decide(Request("bash", {"command": "git status"}, "R2"),
               Context(mode="ask", layers=layers, project_root=str(root),
                       project_trusted=trusted))
    # d.action is "allow", "ask" or "deny"; d.reason says why

m2c/src/m2c/policy/decide.py -- Patch C06: the policy decision function.

    decide(request, context) -> Decision(action, reason, matched_rule, ...)

``action`` is ``allow``, ``ask`` or ``deny``.  The function is PURE (no file or
network access, no clock, no logging, no printing) and TOTAL (it never raises:
any internal failure is a ``deny``).  This is the most security-critical module
of the client, so the whole design is "fail closed":

* An unknown tool, malformed arguments, an unknown mode or risk level, a bad
  project root: ``deny``.
* A shell command that cannot be classified with certainty: ``ask``.
* A settings layer that could not be read safely: nothing is ever ``allow``.
* ``allow`` exists in exactly two forms and the Decision says which in
  ``basis``: ``"rule"`` (an explicit ``allow`` rule matched, named in
  ``matched_rule``) or ``"mode"`` (the permission mode's default says allow for
  this tool and risk class; see modes.py, which never allows a shell command or
  anything above R1).  Every ``allow`` is created by one of two functions
  (``_allow_rule``, ``_allow_mode``) and passes ``_finalize``, which re-checks
  the basis and downgrades anything unexplained to ``deny``.
  tests/policy/test_policy_invariants.py proves this by reading this file.

Order of evaluation for one path or one shell part (first hit wins, and for a
whole shell command the WORST part wins: any deny -> deny, else any ask -> ask,
else allow only when every part is allowed):

m2c/src/m2c/policy/modes.py -- Patch C06: permission modes, the tool catalog the
engine knows, and the default decision per (mode, tool class, risk).

Modes (product guide 8.2, protocol ``common.json#/$defs/mode``):

    plan           reads allowed; every mutation DENIED (``plan_exit`` is the
                   way out, and it asks); no shell.
    ask            reads allowed; edits, deletes and shell ask.   (the default)
    accept-edits   edits to non-protected paths INSIDE the project are allowed;
                   deletes and shell still ask.

A mode default answers only "what happens when no rule says anything".  It can
return ``allow`` in exactly three cases, all for tools that cannot run a process
or reach the network: a read tool at risk R0 (every mode), an edit tool at
risk R1 inside the project in ``accept-edits``, and (Patch L01a) an interact tool
at risk R0 (every mode).  A mode default NEVER allows
network access or process execution: the shell class has no allow entry at all,
and anything above the class ceiling (R3 network or outside the project, R4
irreversible) falls back to ``ask``.  ``tests/policy/test_policy_invariants.py``
enumerates the table to prove that.

The catalog below is a hard-coded copy of ``protocol/v1/tools/*.json`` (P00):
tool name, risk (and ``risk_max`` for ``delete_path``) and the closed set of
arguments.  It is a copy so that deciding never reads a file, and a test fails
if it drifts from the JSON.  The client's risk may RAISE a call's

m2c/src/m2c/policy/rules.py -- Patch C06: permission rules, their layers, and the
purely lexical path checks the policy engine shares.

A rule is ``tool(pattern)`` and has an action, ``deny``, ``ask`` or ``allow``::

    bash(git status)        exact command
    bash(git diff:*)        "git diff" and anything after it (word boundary)
    read_file(src/**)       a path pattern
    edit_file(*.md)         a pattern without a slash also matches the file name

Matching (build plan C06, product guide 8.3):

* Exact strings first, then simple patterns.  ``*`` is the ONLY wildcard and
  matches any run of characters, ``/`` included, so ``src/**`` and ``src/*``
  mean the same.  There is no regular expression anywhere in this module.
* Evaluation order is deny, then ask, then allow, across the UNION of all
  layers (managed, then user, then project).  Because the order is applied to
  the union, a lower layer can never weaken a higher layer: a project ``allow``
  cannot beat a managed ``deny`` or ``ask``, whatever the layer order says.
* Project settings count only when the project is trusted
  (``merge_layers(..., project_trusted=True)``); when it is not, the project
  layer is dropped without being looked at.  The trust prompt itself is built
  later; this module only takes the flag.

Loading is the one place this module touches the disk, and only for the files
the caller names (``load_rule_file`` / ``load_layers`` take paths as arguments,
so tests never read the real home director

m2c/src/m2c/policy/shellparse.py -- Patch C06: a real tokenizer for the subset of
shell syntax the policy engine has to understand.

This is NOT a regex scorer (MiniLocker's engine, which this patch deliberately
does not port, scored command text with regexes and treated syntax it could not
parse as low risk).  It is a small hand-written scanner whose one rule is:

    Anything it cannot classify with certainty is "unknown syntax", and the
    engine turns unknown syntax into ``ask``.  It never turns it into ``allow``.

``parse(command)`` never raises.  It returns a ``ParseResult``: the simple
commands ("parts") found anywhere in the text, in execution order, plus the
reasons (fixed strings, never the command) why some of it is unknown.

What it understands
-------------------
* Separators ``&&  ||  ;  |  |&  &`` and newlines; a part is one simple command.
* Single quotes, double quotes and backslash escapes, and dequoting of words, so
  ``c'u'rl``, ``\curl`` and ``"cur"l`` are all the word ``curl``.  Separators
  inside quotes do not split.
* Subshells ``( )`` and groups ``{ ... ; }`` (flattened: their commands are parts).
* Redirections ``> >> < >| <> &> &>> >& <&`` with an optional fd (``2>&1``) and
  the target word of each.
* Command substitution ``$(...)`` and backticks, nested to a fixed depth: the
  inner text is parsed and its commands become parts that run BEFORE the
  command that contains them.  Substitutions inside double quotes and inside
  ``${...}`` are found
